Chapter 8: Unsupervised Learning Exercises¶

Completed exercises for Chapter 8: grouping data with clustering and spotting unusual faces with density and reconstruction methods. All work uses random_state=42.

A¶

A1¶

Clustering means grouping observations so that similar ones end up in the same group, without using any labels. Classification is different because it learns from labeled examples and then predicts a label for new data. Three clustering algorithms are KMeans, DBSCAN, and Gaussian mixtures.

A2¶

One use is customer segmentation: a store can group shoppers by spending habits and target each group differently. Another use is grouping news articles by topic so readers can browse them. For customer segmentation I would use features like total amount spent and number of visits per month.

A3¶

An elbow plot shows inertia for each k, and you look for the k where the curve bends like an elbow, after which adding clusters helps little. The silhouette score measures how close each point is to its own cluster compared to the nearest other cluster, and higher is better. The smallest inertia alone is not enough because inertia always goes down as k grows, so it would just pick the largest k.

A4¶

Cluster-based label propagation means clustering the data first and then giving all points in a cluster the label of the few labeled points inside it. An incorrect label could spread if a cluster mixes two real groups and the wrong labeled point dominates it. One way to reduce the risk is to only propagate labels in tight, high-confidence clusters and leave uncertain points unlabeled.

A5¶

Two methods that can handle large datasets are Mini-batch KMeans and BIRCH. Two density-based methods are DBSCAN and OPTICS. One limitation is that DBSCAN needs a good eps value and can fail when clusters have very different densities.

A6¶

One example is a doctor labeling rare tumors in medical scans, where each label needs an expert and takes a long time. I would ask the person to label the examples the model is most uncertain about, such as points near cluster borders or with low prediction confidence. To check whether the new labels help, I would retrain the model and compare its accuracy on a held-out set before and after.

A7¶

In outlier detection the training set is assumed to contain both normal and unusual points, and the task is to find the unusual ones inside it. In novelty detection the training set contains only normal points, and the task is to flag new points that look different from them. So the difference is whether the training data is clean or already mixed.

A8¶

A Gaussian mixture models the data as a combination of several bell-shaped distributions, each with its own mean and spread. For clustering, each point is assigned to the Gaussian component that most likely produced it. For anomaly detection, points with very low probability under all components are flagged as unusual.

A9¶

Two approaches are picking the number of components with the lowest BIC, or using cross-validated likelihood on held-out data. A low BIC means the model fits the data well without being too complex. It does not prove the components are the true real-world groups, only that this model describes the data well.¶

A10¶

In [2]:
# A10: one k-means update done by hand, checked with numpy
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

values = np.array([1, 2, 4, 8, 9, 12])
centers = np.array([2.0, 9.0])  # initial centers

# Step 1: assign each value to its nearest center
first_groups = [int(np.argmin([abs(v - c) for c in centers])) for v in values]

# Step 2: new centers are the mean of each group
new_centers = np.array([values[np.array(first_groups) == g].mean() for g in (0, 1)])

# Step 3: assign again with the updated centers
second_groups = [int(np.argmin([abs(v - c) for c in new_centers])) for v in values]
changed = any(f != s for f, s in zip(first_groups, second_groups))

# Step 4: inertia = sum of squared distances, using updated centers and assignments
sq_dist = [(v - new_centers[g]) ** 2 for v, g in zip(values, second_groups)]
inertia = float(np.sum(sq_dist))

table = pd.DataFrame({
    "value": values,
    "first group": first_groups,
    "updated center": np.round([new_centers[g] for g in first_groups], 3),
    "second group": second_groups,
    "squared distance": np.round(sq_dist, 3),
})
print(table.to_string(index=False))
print("\nUpdated centers: 7/3 =", round(7/3, 3), "and 29/3 =", round(29/3, 3))
print("Any point changed groups:", changed)
print("Inertia: 40/3 =", round(40/3, 2))

 value  first group  updated center  second group  squared distance
     1            0           2.333             0             1.778
     2            0           2.333             0             0.111
     4            0           2.333             0             2.778
     8            1           9.667             1             2.778
     9            1           9.667             1             0.444
    12            1           9.667             1             5.444

Updated centers: 7/3 = 2.333 and 29/3 = 9.667
Any point changed groups: False
Inertia: 40/3 = 13.33

If we used six centers, one center could sit on each value, so every distance would be zero and inertia would be zero. But that just memorizes the data instead of summarizing it, so it is not a useful clustering.

# B1: KMeans for k=2..8 on all 500 blobs rows; record inertia and silhouette
rows = []
for k in range(2, 9):
    model = KMeans(n_clusters=k, n_init=10, random_state=42)
    labels = model.fit_predict(blobs)
    rows.append({"k": k, "inertia": round(model.inertia_, 1),
                 "silhouette": round(silhouette_score(blobs, labels), 3)})
b1_table = pd.DataFrame(rows)
print("Split: all 500 blobs rows (no train/test split in B1)")
print(b1_table.to_string(index=False))

plt.figure()
plt.plot(b1_table["k"], b1_table["inertia"], marker="o")
plt.title("Elbow plot: inertia vs k (blobs)")
plt.xlabel("k")
plt.ylabel("inertia")
plt.show()

plt.figure()
plt.plot(b1_table["k"], b1_table["silhouette"], marker="o")
plt.title("Silhouette score vs k (blobs)")
plt.xlabel("k")
plt.ylabel("silhouette score")
plt.show()

Split: all 500 blobs rows (no train/test split in B1)
 k  inertia  silhouette
 2  15385.9       0.607
 3   3125.0       0.782
 4    607.3       0.834
 5    547.8       0.700
 6    492.4       0.564
 7    435.9       0.451
 8    380.5       0.349

I chose k=4. The inertia curve drops steeply from k=3 (3125) to k=4 (607) and then flattens out, which is the elbow. The silhouette score also peaks at k=4 (0.834) and falls for larger k. Both plots agree, so k=4 is the best-supported choice.

In [5]:
# B1: plot the chosen k=4 assignments with centers marked
best_k = 4
model = KMeans(n_clusters=best_k, n_init=10, random_state=42)
labels = model.fit_predict(blobs)
plt.figure()
plt.scatter(blobs["x1"], blobs["x2"], c=labels)
plt.scatter(model.cluster_centers_[:, 0], model.cluster_centers_[:, 1],
            marker="x", s=120, c="black")
plt.title("KMeans assignments with k=4 (x marks centers)")
plt.xlabel("x1")
plt.ylabel("x2")
plt.show()

The four groups look useful: each is a tight, round cloud with its center in the middle, which matches what the eye sees in the scatter plot. But the plots alone cannot tell us what the groups mean in the real world, because the CSV has no labels. Two clouds could still belong to one real category, or one cloud could mix two real categories.

# B2: DBSCAN at four eps values; one plot per setting, same axis limits, noise in gray
from sklearn.cluster import DBSCAN
import numpy as np

x1 = moons["x1"].to_numpy()
x2 = moons["x2"].to_numpy()
x_min, x_max = x1.min() - 0.1, x1.max() + 0.1
y_min, y_max = x2.min() - 0.1, x2.max() + 0.1

for eps in [0.05, 0.10, 0.20, 0.30]:
    db_labels = DBSCAN(eps=eps, min_samples=5).fit_predict(moons)
    colors = ["gray" if lab == -1 else f"C{lab}" for lab in db_labels]
    plt.figure()
    plt.scatter(x1, x2, c=colors, s=8)
    plt.xlim(x_min, x_max)
    plt.ylim(y_min, y_max)
    plt.title(f"DBSCAN on moons (eps={eps}, noise in gray)")
    plt.xlabel("x1")
    plt.ylabel("x2")
    plt.show()
In [8]:
# B2: count clusters (excluding label -1) and noise points for each eps
db_rows = []
for eps in [0.05, 0.10, 0.20, 0.30]:
    db_labels = DBSCAN(eps=eps, min_samples=5).fit_predict(moons)
    n_clusters = len(set(db_labels) - {-1})
    n_noise = int((db_labels == -1).sum())
    db_rows.append({"eps": eps, "n_clusters": n_clusters, "n_noise": n_noise,
                    "pct_noise": round(100 * n_noise / len(db_labels), 1)})
print("Split: all 1000 moons rows")
print(pd.DataFrame(db_rows).to_string(index=False))

Split: all 1000 moons rows
 eps  n_clusters  n_noise  pct_noise
0.05           7       77        7.7
0.10           2        1        0.1
0.20           2        0        0.0
0.30           2        0        0.0

As eps increases, fewer points are called noise and nearby groups merge. At eps=0.05 the crescents shatter into 7 small clusters with 7.7% noise, while eps=0.10 gives 2 clean clusters with only 1 noise point, and larger eps values keep 2 clusters with no noise. The eps=0.10 grouping best follows the crescents because it keeps each crescent whole with almost no noise. KMeans splits them differently because it assumes round clusters around a center, so it cuts each crescent in half instead of following its curve. A noise label does not prove an observation is invalid, it only means the point sits in a low-density gap between dense regions. DBSCAN has no predict method because it never learns cluster centers or boundaries, it only groups the points it was fit on.

C1¶

In [9]:
# C1: load faces, check the data, make the shared 240/80/80 split
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split

faces = pd.read_csv("olivetti_faces.csv")
pixel_cols = [f"pixel_{i}" for i in range(4096)]
print("rows:", faces.shape[0], "| features:", len(pixel_cols))
print("identities:", faces["identity"].nunique(),
      "| images per identity:", sorted(faces["identity"].value_counts().unique()))

X = faces[pixel_cols].to_numpy(dtype=np.float32)
y = faces["identity"].to_numpy()

# 80 test images first, then split the rest into 240 train / 80 validation
X_dev, X_test, y_dev, y_test = train_test_split(
    X, y, test_size=0.20, stratify=y, random_state=42)
X_train, X_val, y_train, y_val = train_test_split(
    X_dev, y_dev, test_size=0.25, stratify=y_dev, random_state=42)

for name, yy in [("train", y_train), ("validation", y_val), ("test", y_test)]:
    counts = np.bincount(yy, minlength=40)
    print(name, "n =", len(yy), "| per identity: min =", counts.min(),
          "max =", counts.max())

# C1: KMeans on the 240 training faces for k = 10..50 (pixel features, no identity used)
face_models = {}
face_rows = []
for k in [10, 20, 30, 40, 50]:
    model = KMeans(n_clusters=k, n_init=10, random_state=42).fit(X_train)
    face_models[k] = model
    face_rows.append({"k": k,
                      "train_inertia": round(model.inertia_, 1),
                      "train_silhouette": round(silhouette_score(X_train, model.labels_), 3)})
face_table = pd.DataFrame(face_rows)
print("Split: training faces (n=240)")
print(face_table.to_string(index=False))

plt.figure()
plt.plot(face_table["k"], face_table["train_inertia"], marker="o")
plt.title("Training inertia vs k (faces)")

plt.ylabel("inertia")
plt.show()

plt.figure()
plt.plot(face_table["k"], face_table["train_silhouette"], marker="o")
plt.title("Training silhouette vs k (faces)")
plt.xlabel("k")
plt.ylabel("silhouette score")
plt.show()

I chose k=50. The silhouette score is highest at k=50 (0.171) and rises across the whole tested range, while inertia shows no sharp elbow. Among the tested values, 50 gives the most separated groups on the training faces.

In [11]:
# C1: show 4 clusters from the k=50 model (up to 10 images each)
# Identity labels are only used here to describe clusters, never for fitting.
model = face_models[50]
sizes = pd.Series(model.labels_).value_counts()
big_enough = sizes[sizes >= 4].index.tolist()
purity = {}
for c in big_enough:
    members = np.flatnonzero(model.labels_ == c)
    purity[c] = np.bincount(y_train[members], minlength=40).max() / len(members)
coherent = max(big_enough, key=lambda c: (purity[c], sizes[c]))
mixed = min(big_enough, key=lambda c: (purity[c], -sizes[c]))
show = [coherent, mixed] + [c for c in sizes.index if c not in (coherent, mixed)][:2]
print("Split: training faces (n=240); k=50")
for c in show:
    print(f"cluster {c}: size = {sizes[c]}, identity purity = {purity.get(c, 0):.2f}")

fig, axes = plt.subplots(4, 10, figsize=(13, 6))
for row, c in enumerate(show):
    members = np.flatnonzero(model.labels_ == c)
    for col in range(10):
        ax = axes[row, col]
        ax.axis("off")
        if col < len(members):
            ax.imshow(X_train[members[col]].reshape(64, 64), cmap="gray", vmin=0, vmax=1)
            ax.set_title(str(members[col]), fontsize=7)
    axes[row, 0].set_ylabel(f"cluster {c}\n(n={sizes[c]})", rotation=0, labelpad=30)
fig.suptitle("Training faces from four k=50 clusters (titles are training row numbers)")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

Split: training faces (n=240); k=50
cluster 33: size = 6, identity purity = 1.00
cluster 5: size = 10, identity purity = 0.20
cluster 26: size = 11, identity purity = 0.55
cluster 38: size = 9, identity purity = 0.44

Cluster 33 is coherent: all 6 faces show the same person in a similar front-facing pose, so pixel similarity lined up with identity here. Cluster 5 is mixed: 10 faces of different people, but most are smiling broadly with teeth showing, so the group formed around expression instead of identity. Cluster 26 is mostly faces wearing glasses, while cluster 38 mixes neutral faces of several people. The groups seem to follow glasses, smiles, and lighting as much as identity. That is why k does not have to equal 40: KMeans groups by pixel similarity, not by person, and one person's 10 photos vary in pose, lighting, and expression while different people can share glasses or a smile.

In [12]:
# C2: baseline classifier on raw training pixels; check for convergence warnings
import warnings
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
from sklearn.metrics import accuracy_score
from sklearn.exceptions import ConvergenceWarning

base = LogisticRegression(C=1.0, max_iter=5000)
with warnings.catch_warnings(record=True) as caught:
    warnings.simplefilter("always", ConvergenceWarning)
    base.fit(X_train, y_train)
warned = any(issubclass(w.category, ConvergenceWarning) for w in caught)
base_val = accuracy_score(y_val, base.predict(X_val))
print("Split: validation faces (n=80)")
print("baseline (raw pixels) val accuracy:", round(base_val, 3))
print("convergence warning:", warned, "(max_iter=5000 was enough, no change needed)")

Split: validation faces (n=80)
baseline (raw pixels) val accuracy: 0.963
convergence warning: False (max_iter=5000 was enough, no change needed)
In [13]:
# C2: distance features and combined features for each k
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler

c2_rows = [{"representation": "raw_pixels", "k": "-", "n_features": 4096,
             "val_accuracy": round(base_val, 3)}]
for k in [10, 20, 30, 40, 50]:
    km = face_models[k]  # reuse the C1 model: same settings and same training data
    d_train, d_val = km.transform(X_train), km.transform(X_val)
    scaler = StandardScaler().fit(d_train)  # fit on train distances only
    clf = LogisticRegression(C=1.0, max_iter=5000).fit(scaler.transform(d_train), y_train)
    c2_rows.append({"representation": "distances", "k": k, "n_features": k,
                    "val_accuracy": round(accuracy_score(
                        y_val, clf.predict(scaler.transform(d_val))), 3)})
    comb_train = np.column_stack([X_train, d_train])  # unscaled distances after pixels
    comb_val = np.column_stack([X_val, d_val])
    scaler2 = StandardScaler().fit(comb_train)  # fresh scaler on combined train only
    clf2 = LogisticRegression(C=1.0, max_iter=5000).fit(scaler2.transform(comb_train), y_train)
    c2_rows.append({"representation": "pixels_plus_distances", "k": k,
                    "n_features": 4096 + k,
                    "val_accuracy": round(accuracy_score(
                        y_val, clf2.predict(scaler2.transform(comb_val))), 3)})
print("Split: validation faces (n=80)")
print(pd.DataFrame(c2_rows).to_string(index=False))

Split: validation faces (n=80)
       representation  k  n_features  val_accuracy
           raw_pixels  -        4096         0.963
            distances 10          10         0.613
pixels_plus_distances 10        4106         0.950
            distances 20          20         0.800
pixels_plus_distances 20        4116         0.950
            distances 30          30         0.838
pixels_plus_distances 30        4126         0.963
            distances 40          40         0.863
pixels_plus_distances 40        4136         0.950
            distances 50          50         0.875
pixels_plus_distances 50        4146         0.950

The tie for best validation accuracy (0.963) is between raw pixels and pixels_plus_distances with k=30. I chose raw pixels because it is simpler: one classifier on the original features, with no KMeans model and no extra scaler to maintain. The extra 30 distance features added nothing beyond the baseline. Note that the combined experiment changes both the representation and the scaling compared with the raw-pixel baseline, so its result is not a pure test of cluster features.

In [14]:
# C2: evaluate the chosen baseline system once on the test split
test_pred = base.predict(X_test)
test_acc = accuracy_score(y_test, test_pred)
print("Split: test faces (n=80), evaluated once")
print("test accuracy:", round(test_acc, 3))
print("correct:", int((test_pred == y_test).sum()), "of", len(y_test))

Split: test faces (n=80), evaluated once
test accuracy: 0.95
correct: 76 of 80

Cluster features helped the distance-only representation a lot: its validation accuracy rose from 0.613 at k=10 to 0.875 at k=50, as more centers gave a finer map of face space. But they did not beat the raw-pixel baseline, and the combined representation only tied it at k=30. So the k that looked best for clustering (k=50, highest silhouette) is not the k that helped classification most (k=30 for the combined features). Clustering quality and classification usefulness are different goals.

from sklearn.decomposition import PCA

pca = PCA(n_components=0.99, svd_solver="full", random_state=42).fit(X_train)
print("components kept:", pca.n_components_)
print("retained variance:", round(float(pca.explained_variance_ratio_.sum()), 4))
Z_train = pca.transform(X_train)
Z_val = pca.transform(X_val)

components kept: 176
retained variance: 0.9901
In [16]:
# C3: try GMM sizes 1, 2, 5, 10 on the reduced training data
from sklearn.mixture import GaussianMixture

gmm_rows = []
gmms = {}
for n_comp in [1, 2, 5, 10]:
    gmm = GaussianMixture(n_components=n_comp, covariance_type="diag", n_init=5,
                          max_iter=300, reg_covar=1e-5, random_state=42).fit(Z_train)
    gmms[n_comp] = gmm
    gmm_rows.append({"n_components": n_comp, "converged": gmm.converged_,
                     "BIC": round(gmm.bic(Z_train), 1), "AIC": round(gmm.aic(Z_train), 1)})
print("Split: PCA-reduced training faces (n=240)")
print(pd.DataFrame(gmm_rows).to_string(index=False))
best_n = min([r for r in gmm_rows if r["converged"]], key=lambda r: r["BIC"])["n_components"]
print("selected (converged, lowest BIC): n_components =", best_n)
gmm = gmms[best_n]

# C3: generate 12 faces from the selected GMM and show them
gen, _ = gmm.sample(12)
gen_images = pca.inverse_transform(gen).reshape(-1, 64, 64)

fig, axes = plt.subplots(3, 4, figsize=(8, 6))
for ax, img in zip(axes.flat, gen_images):
    ax.imshow(np.clip(img, 0, 1), cmap="gray", vmin=0, vmax=1)  # clip only for display
    ax.axis("off")
fig.suptitle("12 faces sampled from the selected GMM")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

The generated faces look blurred because the GMM draws random samples from smooth Gaussian blobs in PCA space, and the inverse transform blends many eigenfaces together. Real faces have sharp edges and fine detail that an average of training faces cannot reproduce.

In [18]:
# C3: modify the first 12 validation faces (on 64x64 images) and score all groups
def make_groups(images):
    imgs64 = images.reshape(-1, 64, 64)
    return {
        "original": images,
        "rot90": np.rot90(imgs64, axes=(1, 2)).reshape(-1, 4096),
        "fliplr": np.fliplr(imgs64).reshape(-1, 4096),
        "dark": (imgs64 * 0.5).reshape(-1, 4096),
    }

val12 = make_groups(X_val[:12])
score_rows = []
for name, imgs in val12.items():
    scores = gmm.score_samples(pca.transform(imgs))
    score_rows.append({"group": name, "n": len(imgs),
                       "mean_log_density": round(float(scores.mean()), 1),
                       "min_log_density": round(float(scores.min()), 1)})
print("Split: first 12 validation faces and their synthetic modifications")
print(pd.DataFrame(score_rows).to_string(index=False))

plt.figure()
plt.boxplot([gmm.score_samples(pca.transform(imgs)) for imgs in val12.values()],
            tick_labels=list(val12.keys()))
plt.title("GMM log density: original vs modified (12 validation faces)")
plt.ylabel("log density")
plt.show()

# C3: freeze the model and threshold, then score the test split once
test_groups = make_groups(X_test)
print("Split: all 80 test faces and their synthetic modifications (frozen threshold)")
for name, imgs in test_groups.items():
    scores = gmm.score_samples(pca.transform(imgs))
    print(name, "flagged:", round(float((scores < threshold).mean() * 100), 1), "%")

The GMM flagged the rotated and flipped faces well: 100% of test rotations and 98.8% of test flips fell below the frozen threshold. It failed on the darkened faces: 0% were flagged on the test split, and their average log density was actually higher than the originals. So geometric changes that move a face off the learned manifold are caught, while a global brightness change is not. These modifications are synthetic test cases, not real defects, so the rates only show how this model reacts to these specific changes.

# C4: PCA reconstruction error (MSE over 4096 pixels, no clipping before the error)
def recon_error(images):
    return ((images - pca.inverse_transform(pca.transform(images))) ** 2).mean(axis=1)

val12_err = {name: recon_error(imgs) for name, imgs in val12.items()}

# C4: input/reconstruction pairs: an original, a high-error rotation, a hard-to-flag darkening
high_rot = int(np.argmax(test_err["rot90"]))   # worst reconstructed rotation
dark_idx = int(np.argmin(test_err["dark"]))    # darkening is hard to flag
pairs = [("input: original", X_test[0]),
         ("input: rot90 (high error)", test_groups["rot90"][high_rot]),
         ("input: dark x0.5 (hard to flag)", test_groups["dark"][dark_idx])]

fig, axes = plt.subplots(3, 2, figsize=(6, 9))
for row, (title, img) in enumerate(pairs):
    recon = pca.inverse_transform(pca.transform(img.reshape(1, -1))).reshape(64, 64)
    axes[row, 0].imshow(img.reshape(64, 64), cmap="gray", vmin=0, vmax=1)
    axes[row, 0].set_title(title)
    axes[row, 0].axis("off")
    axes[row, 1].imshow(recon, cmap="gray", vmin=0, vmax=1)
    axes[row, 1].set_title("reconstruction")
    axes[row, 1].axis("off")
fig.suptitle("Input vs PCA reconstruction (test faces)")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

On the test split, the GMM flagged 100% of rotations and 98.8% of flips but 0% of darkened faces, and PCA reconstruction error flagged 100% of rotations, 100% of flips, and 0% of darkened faces. Both methods catch the geometric changes and both miss the darkening. A darkened face keeps a small reconstruction error because multiplying every pixel by 0.5 is a change the PCA subspace already handles well: brightness shifts are captured by the top components, so the reconstruction follows the darkening and little error remains. A modification that stays near the PCA subspace will always be hard to flag with reconstruction error.

Final interpretation¶

For compact round groups I would choose KMeans: on the blobs data k=4 gave a clear elbow and the highest silhouette (0.834), but KMeans assumes spherical clusters, so it fails on curved shapes. For curved groups I would choose DBSCAN: at eps=0.10 it recovered the two crescents almost perfectly, but it needs a good eps value and has no predict method for new points. For unusual face images I would use PCA reconstruction error: it flagged 100% of the rotated and flipped test faces with a simple frozen threshold, but it missed the darkened faces entirely because brightness changes stay inside the PCA subspace. None of these rates are guaranteed: they come from my own synthetic modifications and my own validation split, and real unusual images could behave differently.
